## 5.10.14 Operational Readiness: Runbooks, SLOs, and the Pre-Launch Checklist

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** · Prerequisites: metrics, alerting, on-call practice

**Definition:** operational readiness is the state in which a service can be run by someone who did not build it, at 3am, without the author on the phone. It has three components: **instrumentation** (metrics and dashboards you can read), **objectives** (a measurable target and the error budget it implies), and **procedures** (a runbook per alert and a pre-launch checklist that gates the release).

**SLI, SLO, and error budget — the vocabulary you must use precisely**
```
SLI   a measured quantity: "the proportion of valid requests served successfully,
      measured over 30 days, excluding 429s" or "p99 latency under 300 ms for
      /checkout". The *measurement definition* is the hard part and the part
      most teams skip.
SLO   the target for an SLI: 99.9% of valid requests return non-5xx within 300 ms.
      An SLO is a promise to users, chosen by engineering + product together.
Budget  1 - SLO. With 99.9%, your monthly budget is 0.1% of requests. It is the
      currency you spend on releases: every risky deploy spends budget, and when
      it is exhausted you freeze features and fix reliability.
```
Why this matters more than "we have alerts": **an SLO converts reliability into a planning tool.** Without one, every engineer has a different opinion about whether a 1% error spike is shippable. With one, the question is answered by arithmetic.

**Error budgets and release policy — a concrete example**
```
99.9% monthly SLO on the availability SLI, ~40M requests/month
  budget: ~40,000 failed requests

14:00  budget 60% remaining   -> ship normally
14:00  budget 20% remaining   -> fixes and stabilisation only, no feature flags on prod
14:00  budget exhausted       -> release freeze; the team works reliability until the
                                 budget recovers (windowed burn rate matters, not the
                                 monthly number, so recovery is measured properly)
```
The policy is the deliverable, not the number. It must be agreed by the team that has to live with it, or it will be quietly ignored.

**Burn-rate alerting, and why a single threshold does not work.** Alerting on "error rate > 1%" pages you for both a catastrophic outage and a slow trickle. Burn-rate alerting pages on how fast you are consuming the budget, over multiple windows, which distinguishes the two:
```
Fast burn (page):   14.4x budget burn over 1h AND 5m     -> ~2% of budget in an hour
                     page, because this burns a month of budget in a day
Slow burn (ticket): 6x budget burn over 6h AND 30m        -> investigate during the day
                     AND 3x over 3d                      -> a week-long problem

Plus one multiwindow, multi-burn-rate rule, and a "budget remaining" dashboard.
The 5-minute-window condition is what stops you paging when the incident is already over.
```
This is the single highest-leverage alerting change most teams can make: it converts "error rate is high" into "we are failing our users at a rate that matters, and here is the burn".

**What to alert on, and what not to.** Alert on **symptoms the user feels**, not on causes you can infer:
```
ALERT: availability burn rate, latency burn rate, error-budget exhaustion
ALERT: queue depth and OLDEST MESSAGE AGE (depth alone lies: a deep queue draining
       steadily is fine; 3 messages stuck for an hour is an incident)
ALERT: job last-success age (catches the silently-dead cron)
ALERT: certificate expiry (< 14 days), secrets rotation overdue
ALERT: replication lag, disk space, connection-pool saturation
TICKET: individual 5xx from one upstream, slow growth of a queue, a single region degraded
LOG-QUERY: a new error signature appearing at all
NEVER: CPU at 80%, memory at 75%, "disk usage changed", a single request failure
```
A `CPU > 80%` alert trains the team to ignore alerts, which is worse than having none.

**The runbook: what one actually contains**
```
1. Title + one-sentence statement of what breaks and who is affected
2. Severity and the alert that fires it (link)
3. Dashboard links (the exact panels, not the dashboard index)
4. Detection: how this looks in metrics, logs, and traces
5. Diagnosis: a decision tree or an ordered list of queries to run
     SELECT ... ;  -- copy-pasteable, parameterised, with a default time range
6. Mitigation: what to do RIGHT NOW, with the exact command, in order, with
   expected output at each step. Most mitigations are: roll back, disable a flag,
   shed load, restart, fail over.
7. Escalation: who, when to page them, after how long
8. Verification: how to confirm it is actually fixed (the query, the panel, the check)
9. Rollback/undo: how to undo the mitigation itself
10. Known gotchas and history: what has fooled you before
```
The test of a runbook: **hand it to someone who has never seen the service and time how long until they are effective.** If it takes more than 15 minutes, rewrite it. A runbook without step 6 (exact commands) is a document, not a runbook.

**The pre-launch checklist — the gate, not the wish list**
```
Design & correctness
  [ ] Error contract, pagination contract, idempotency, and authz reviewed (5.10.9)
  [ ] Every new endpoint in the API docs with an owner
  [ ] Backwards compatibility checked by the CI diff gate
  [ ] Feature flags default OFF in production, with an owner and an expiry

Data
  [ ] Migration is expand/contract, reversible, and has been run on a production-sized copy
  [ ] Backfill has a resume cursor, batching, a rate limit, and a kill switch
  [ ] Indexes created CONCURRENTLY where the table is large
  [ ] Retention/purge behaviour verified for every new table

Observability
  [ ] RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) per endpoint, per service
  [ ] A dashboard exists and someone other than the author has read it
  [ ] The SLO is defined and measured; the burn-rate alert is wired
  [ ] Structured logs with correlation ids and redaction verified
  [ ] Business metrics for the feature's success AND its failure (a launch with no
      business metric cannot be evaluated, only argued about)

Operational
  [ ] Runbook written for every new alert, and rehearsed
  [ ] On-call ownership and escalation are defined (CODEOWNERS)
  [ ] Capacity: has this been load tested at 2x expected peak with the new query pattern?
  [ ] Rollback plan exists and has been rehearsed — a rollback that has never been run
      is a hypothesis
  [ ] Deploy is progressive (canary or blue/green) with an automatic rollback trigger
  [ ] Dependency inventory is complete: what new third parties does this add?
  [ ] Security review: authz on every new route, secret handling, upload paths, injection

Communication
  [ ] Support and CS briefed on user-visible changes
  [ ] Customer-facing changes have a comms plan and a rollback comms plan
  [ ] Launch monitoring owner for the first 48 hours is named
```
The last section is the one nobody has and the one that determines whether the first 48 hours go well.

**Trade-offs**
- **SLIs vs raw metrics.** A full user-journey SLI ("can a user complete checkout") is the most honest and the hardest; per-endpoint availability is easy and can be green while the journey is broken. Use both: per-endpoint for diagnosis, journey-level for the SLO.
- **Strict SLOs vs pragmatic ones.** 99.99% for a hobby project means a 4-minute monthly budget and a feature freeze every month. 99.5% is often honest and sustainable. Pick the SLO you will actually defend.
- **Checklists vs judgement.** A 60-item checklist gets skipped. Gate the top 8 items in CI and keep the rest as a review conversation.
- **Runbooks written before launch vs after the first incident.** Before, if you can. After, if you must — but then write it the day it burns you, while the details are fresh.
- **Game days vs real incidents.** A deliberate failure on a Tuesday is worth ten postmortems, because the runbook gets tested where you can still ask questions.

**Common mistakes**
- An SLO nobody agreed to, so it is not used to make decisions.
- Alerting on causes (CPU, memory) instead of symptoms.
- A single-threshold error-rate alert that pages for a trickle.
- Runbooks that are links to dashboards rather than procedures.
- No rollback rehearsal, so the first real rollback fails for a reason nobody predicted.
- A launch with a technical metric and no business metric.
- No named owner for the first 48 hours after launch.
- Treating the checklist as paperwork rather than as gates.

**What an interviewer probes**
🟡 "What is an error budget and how would you use it?" 🟡 "What makes a good alert?" (A symptom, with a threshold that means something, and a link to the runbook.) 🔴 "Define an SLI and SLO for a checkout service." (Successful valid requests excluding 429 and client errors, over 30 days; plus checkout-completion rate; target 99.9%; budget ~0.1%.) 🔴 "Your error rate is 0.4%. Do you ship?" (Only with context: current burn vs the window, whether it is a known cause, whether the change is reversible, and what the budget position is. An answer that is yes or no without that reasoning is the wrong answer.) 🔴 "Your p99 is 900 ms and your SLO is 300 ms. Why has nobody been paged?" (Wrong threshold, or alerting on the average, or a SLI that measures the wrong thing, or the alert routed to a dashboard nobody watches.) ⚫ "Your SLO is 99.9%, and a dependency pushes errors to 2% for 30 minutes. Walk me through the alert, the response, and the follow-up." (Multiwindow burn-rate alert fires on the 1h condition; the on-call runs the runbook; mitigation is the breaker plus a flag plus shedding; the postmortem asks whether the dependency should have been behind a timeout, whether the error budget policy should have frozen releases, and whether the runbook was current.)

**Mistakes:** unagreed SLOs; cause-based alerts; single-threshold paging; non-procedural runbooks; unrehearsed rollbacks; no business metrics.

**Mini task:** write an SLO and error-budget policy for one of your services, implement a two-window burn-rate alert, write a full runbook for one existing alert, then run a 20-minute game day where you kill the primary dependency and follow the runbook with someone who has never seen the service.

---

## 5.10.15 Deprecation, Versioning, and Killing a Feature Safely

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know** → ⚫ Expert (sunset mechanics, consumer telemetry, internal deprecation)

**Definition:** deprecation is the managed retirement of an interface or behaviour: you announce it, you measure who still uses it, you migrate consumers, you enforce a date, and you remove it. Versioning is one *mechanism* for deprecation; it is not the process, and the process is the part that actually gets skipped.

**Versioning strategies, honestly compared**
| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| URL path (`/v1`, `/v2`) | Version in the path | Obvious in logs and browsers; easy to route and to test; clients can pin a version | Coarse: a tiny change forks the whole surface; encourages "version everything"; leaves v1 alive forever |
| Header (`Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2`) | Media type in `Accept` | Resource URLs stay clean; can serve several versions from one handler | Invisible in a URL bar; easy for a client library to omit; hard to eyeball in access logs |
| Query parameter | `?version=2` | Trivial | Caches key on it; treated as a distinct resource everywhere; ugly |
| Additive-only, never version | No versions; only backwards-compatible changes | No version debt; forces discipline; best client ergonomics | Requires an extremely strict compatibility gate; slow to adopt a genuinely breaking redesign |
| Internal-only versioning | Versions between your own services | Free, since you control both ends | Not for external APIs; internal APIs leak outward via SDKs |

**The recommendation, and the reasoning you should be able to give:** for a **public API**, do additive-only changes plus a `Sunset` header for the rare breaking change, and reserve a major version for a genuine redesign — not for a rename. For **internal services**, version aggressively and freely, because you control both ends and a coordinated deploy is possible. Most teams do the opposite of this and end up with three public versions and zero internal ones.

**Deprecation is a five-step process, and the steps are the deliverable**
```
1. DECIDE   Write the reason and the alternative. "Deprecated because the v1 webhook
            cannot sign payloads; use v2." "Deprecated because of a security fix in
            the underlying library" are useful. "Deprecated" is not.
2. ANNOUNCE In the response headers (machine-readable), in the docs, and in the product:
              Deprecation: true
              Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT      (RFC 8594)
              Link: <https://docs.example.com/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"
            Email every registered consumer with usage numbers, not a generic notice.
            A banner in the developer dashboard showing YOUR usage of the deprecated
            endpoint is the single most effective announcement there is.
3. MEASURE  Per-consumer usage telemetry, exported to a dashboard and emailed weekly:
            who called it, how often, last call time, and their plan tier. You cannot
            migrate what you cannot see, and "we deprecated it and someone broke"
            is a support incident you chose to create.
4. MIGRATE  Provide a migration path that is easier than staying: a compatibility shim,
            a codemod, a self-serve migration tool, a migration deadline before the
            deadline. Deprecation without a migration path is an ultimatum.
5. ENFORCE  After the sunset date, respond 410 Gone with a pointer — not 404 (which
            looks like a bug and generates tickets) and not 200 with a warning body
            (which nobody reads). Then delete the code, the tests, and the docs.
```
**410 vs 404 vs 501 is worth stating explicitly**, because it is a small thing that shows you have thought about it:
```
404 Not Found     "I have never heard of this resource." Correct after removal.
410 Gone          "This resource existed and has been removed. Here is the replacement."
                  The only correct response to a post-sunset client, and it is
                  what makes the failure self-diagnosing in the client's logs.
501 Not Implemented  "This method/feature is recognised but not supported here." Correct
                  when you keep the path but disable the behaviour.
```

**Killing a feature safely — the order matters more than the decision**
```
Step 1  STOP NEW USAGE. Set the feature flag to OFF for everyone (5.10.12). This is
        reversible and is the step that tells you how badly people depended on it.
        Watch metrics for a week. A feature nobody missed was already dead.
Step 2  COMMUNICATE WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, in the product, not just the changelog:
        what disappears, what replaces it, when, and what happens to their data.
        "This feature is deprecated" is not a product announcement; "Checkout v1 will
        stop working on 1 March; your carts will be preserved; here is the migration"
        is.
Step 3  MIGRATE DATA. Every user has something in the old shape: a saved cart, a
        configured integration, an API key, a report definition. Migrating data is a
        much larger project than removing code, and it is the step teams forget.
        It needs a backfill, a validation query ("no user has an unmigrated cart"),
        and a rollback.
Step 4  FREEZE. Set the old path read-only. No new writes. Now you can detect stragglers
        without risking data loss.
Step 5  REMOVE. Delete the code, the tables (after retention), the jobs, the flags, the
        docs, the dashboards. Then remove the "off" path so it cannot be resurrected
        by a stale flag.
```
Step 5 is the one most teams skip, and skipping it is why codebases accumulate a "legacy" folder that nobody dares delete and that still has bugs in it.

**Internal deprecation: the same discipline for code, not just APIs.** Internal APIs have callers you cannot see, including batch jobs, scripts, and other teams' cron containers. The mechanism is the same: annotate, measure, and make the compiler tell you.
```ts
/** @deprecated since 2026-02-01. Use `getUserScoped(tenantId, id)` — this version does not
 *  scope by tenant. Removal after 2026-08-01. Ticket OPS-4412. */
/* eslint-disable @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated */
export async function getUser(id: string) { return repo.users.findById(id); }
```
A deprecation that produces a **compiler warning** and a **usage report from the build** ("this function is called from 3 repositories, listed here") is a deprecation with a completion mechanism. A deprecation that is a comment in a wiki is a wish.

**Trade-offs**
- **Additive-only vs major versions.** Additive-only avoids version debt entirely and is the best long-term answer, but it constrains you: you can never change a shape, only add. That constraint is real and should be accepted deliberately, not discovered.
- **Long support windows vs a moving codebase.** A 24-month deprecation window is generous to consumers and expensive for you (N-1 maintenance, doubled test matrix, security patching twice). Twelve months is a common compromise. The right number depends on your customers' release cycle, so ask, do not assume.
- **Silently breaking vs loudly failing.** Silent breakage produces angry customers and a hard debugging session. A loud 410 with a pointer produces a self-diagnosing client error and a support ticket that takes two minutes. Loud always wins, provided the loudness is actionable.
- **Deleting data vs keeping it read-only.** Deleting is clean and is often a compliance requirement; keeping it read-only for a defined period is kinder to users who need to migrate. Decide the retention explicitly, and honour an erasure request inside it.
- **Flags vs versions for a behaviour change.** A flag can be turned off instantly and targeted at a cohort; a version cannot. Use a flag for behaviour and a version for shape, and do not use a version to ship a behaviour change "safely".

**Common mistakes**
- Deprecating with a changelog entry and no measurement of who is affected.
- No `Sunset` date, so it never actually ends.
- Removing the code without migrating the data, so users lose their carts/integrations.
- Responding 404 after removal, which generates support tickets instead of self-diagnosing errors.
- Keeping the "off" path after removal, so the feature can be resurrected by a stale flag.
- A deprecation with no alternative provided.
- Internal deprecation with no build-level usage report, so nobody knows who still calls it.
- Running v1 and v2 forever because nobody owns the migration.

**What an interviewer probes**
🟢 "How do you deprecate an API endpoint?" 🟡 "What headers do you send when deprecating?" (`Deprecation`, `Sunset`, `Link rel="deprecation"`.) 🟡 "404 or 410 after removal, and why?" 🔴 "You need to remove `POST /v1/charges`. Walk me through the process." (Usage telemetry first; announce with a date and an alternative; migrate; 410 after sunset; then delete code and data. Explicitly: what about existing saved payment methods? That is a data migration, not a code change.) 🔴 "You deprecated an endpoint and a big customer broke. What did you miss?" (No per-consumer usage data; no direct notification; no migration path; a sunset date inside their freeze window.) 🔴 "Your API has v1, v2, and v3. How do you get to one version?" (Pick the newest as canonical, make v2 and v1 additive-compatible with it where possible, publish usage telemetry per version, set a sunset date, and offer a codemod. Do not announce a v4.) ⚫ "Design the deprecation of a legacy webhook for 40,000 registered endpoints." (Per-endpoint usage telemetry including last-delivery time and failure rate; tiered communication by usage; a signature-compatible shim so the migration is a URL change; a sandbox for verification; a 90-day window with weekly reminders; 410 with a signed migration guide; and a grandfathered exception process for the top ten accounts with named owners and dates.)

**Mistakes:** no measurement; no sunset date; data not migrated; 404 after removal; dead path kept; no alternative; internal deprecation without usage data.

**Mini task:** pick one endpoint in your API, add the three deprecation headers, build per-consumer usage telemetry for it, write the migration guide, and dry-run the whole thing with a fake consumer — including the 410 response.

# 5.10 MUST-IMPLEMENT-FROM-SCRATCH (8 Problems)

**How to practice:** write each from memory on a blank file, then test against the edge cases listed. In an interview, state your assumptions out loud, implement the main path, then *say* which edge cases you would handle next — reasoning about edges is what separates a mid-level from a senior. Each of these fits in 30-50 minutes and each proves one of the eight canonical practices concretely rather than as vocabulary.

These eight are the highest-leverage exercises in this part. They are ordered so each one builds on the last: config (1) feeds the logger (2), which the validation middleware (3) uses for error reporting, which paginates (4), which soft-deletes (5) and audits (6), which are both tenant-scoped (7) and made safe to retry (8).

---

### 1. A twelve-factor config loader: layered precedence, fail-fast, redaction

**The contract:** config comes from layered sources with a documented precedence; every value is typed and validated; the object is loaded once, frozen, and never re-read; missing or invalid values produce one aggregated error naming every problem; secrets are redacted in any rendered form; cross-field rules are enforced.

```ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export type Config = ReturnType<typeof buildSchema>;

const csv = z.string().transform(s => s.split(',').map(x => s.trim()).filter(Boolean));

// --- 1. The schema, with types, bounds, and cross-field rules -----------------
function buildSchema(env: string) {
  const strict = env === 'production';
  return z.object({
    NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'staging', 'production']),
    PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
    HOST: z.string().default('0.0.0.0'),

    LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(['trace', 'debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error', 'fatal']).default('info'),
    LOG_PRETTY: z.preprocess(v => v === 'true', z.boolean()).default(false),

    DATABASE_URL: z.string().url().refine(u => /^postgres(ql)?:/.test(u), 'must be a postgres URL'),
    DB_POOL_MAX: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(500).default(20),

    REDIS_URL: z.string().url().optional(),

    SESSION_SECRET: z.string().min(32, 'must be at least 32 chars for scrypt'),
    COOKIE_DOMAIN: z.string().optional(),

    RATE_LIMIT_RPM: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100_000).default(600),
    FEATURE_FLAGS: csv.default(''),
    ALLOWED_ORIGINS: csv.default(''),
    EMERGENCY_DISABLE: csv.default(''),

    SENTRY_DSN: z.string().url().optional(),
  }).superRefine((c, ctx) => {
    // Cross-field rules are where the real bugs live.
    if (strict && c.SESSION_SECRET.startsWith('dev')) {
      ctx.addIssue({ code: 'custom', path: ['SESSION_SECRET'], message: 'development secret in production' });
    }
    if (strict && c.LOG_PRETTY) {
      ctx.addIssue({ code: 'custom', path: ['LOG_PRETTY'], message: 'pretty logging is not allowed in production' });
    }
    if (strict && c.ALLOWED_ORIGINS === '') {
      ctx.addIssue({ code: 'custom', path: ['ALLOWED_ORIGINS'], message: 'empty origin allowlist is a CORS footgun' });
    }
    if (strict && c.DB_POOL_MAX * 20 > 1000) {
      ctx.addIssue({ code: 'custom', path: ['DB_POOL_MAX'], message: 'pool size implies more than 1000 server connections' });
    }
  });
}

// --- 2. Layered sources, lowest precedence first -----------------------------
export function buildConfig(layers: Record<string, string>[] = []): Config {
  // Layers are applied in order, so a later layer overwrites an earlier one.
  // The env layer is always last, which is factor III: the environment wins.
  const merged: Record<string, string> = {};
  for (const layer of layers) Object.assign(merged, layer);
  Object.assign(merged, process.env);

  const parsed = buildSchema(merged.NODE_ENV ?? 'development').safeParse(merged);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    // Aggregate EVERY issue. Reporting one at a time turns one restart into five.
    const detail = parsed.error.issues
      .map(i => `  - ${i.path.join('.') || '(root)'}: ${i.message}`)
      .join('\n');
    throw new ConfigurationError(`Invalid configuration:\n${detail}`, parsed.error.issues);
  }
  return Object.freeze(parsed.data);
}

export class ConfigurationError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, readonly issues: z.ZodIssue[]) { super(message); this.name = 'ConfigurationError'; }
}

// --- 3. Load once, lazily, and freeze ---------------------------------------
let instance: Config | undefined;
export function config(): Config {
  instance ??= buildConfig();
  return instance;
}

// --- 4. Redaction, so logging config can never leak a secret ----------------
const SECRET_KEYS = new Set(['SESSION_SECRET', 'DATABASE_URL', 'REDIS_URL', 'SENTRY_DSN']);
export function redactedConfig(c: Config = config()): Record<string, unknown> {
  const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(c)) {
    if (!SECRET_KEYS.has(k)) { out[k] = v; continue; }
    // Show enough to identify WHICH secret without revealing it.
    const s = String(v ?? '');
    out[k] = s ? `${s.slice(0, 4)}…${s.slice(-2)} (len ${s.length})` : null;
  }
  return out;
}

// --- 5. Startup assertions: the invariants that must hold for this process ---
export async function assertStartupSafety(c: Config = config()) {
  const problems: string[] = [];

  if (c.REDIS_URL && new URL(c.REDIS_URL).protocol !== 'redis:') problems.push('REDIS_URL is not redis:');

  // Verify the real dependency exists, with a short timeout, at boot.
  const started = Date.now();
  try {
    const r = await fetch(`${c.SENTRY_DSN ? '' : ''}`, {}).catch(() => null); // placeholder for real checks
    void r;
  } catch { /* handled by caller */ }

  // Noisy-neighbour math you want to know about before traffic arrives.
  if (c.DB_POOL_MAX > 100) problems.push(`DB_POOL_MAX=${c.DB_POOL_MAX} is very high for a small database`);

  if (problems.length) throw new ConfigurationError(`Unsafe startup:\n  - ${problems.join('\n  - ')}`, []);
  return { checkedIn: Date.now() - started };
}

// --- 6. Test helpers --------------------------------------------------------
export function withEnv(env: Record<string, string>, fn: () => void) {
  const before = { ...process.env };
  for (const k of Object.keys(process.env)) if (!(k in env)) delete process.env[k];
  Object.assign(process.env, env);
  try { fn(); } finally {
    for (const k of Object.keys(process.env)) delete process.env[k];
    Object.assign(process.env, before);
    instance = undefined;
  }
}
```

*Edge cases:* `PORT=0` (valid — means "let the OS choose", so `min(1)` is arguably wrong and `min(0)` with a special case is better); `LOG_LEVEL=` (empty string fails the enum rather than defaulting, because `.default()` only applies to `undefined`); a numeric var set to `""` (`z.coerce.number()` gives `0`, which then fails `min(1)` — good); `NODE_ENV=prod` (fails the enum, which is correct); a secret with exactly 32 chars; `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` with trailing commas and spaces; a production config where `SESSION_SECRET` is 32 chars of `dev…`.

*Follow-ups:* how would you implement hot reload without breaking immutability (load → validate → atomic swap, and only for the subset that is reloadable); how would you support a config file layer that is itself validated; how you would generate documentation from the schema so the README cannot drift.

---

### 2. A structured logger with levels, redaction, request context, and sampling

**The contract:** JSON lines; a level that is validated and switchable at runtime; per-line request/trace context via `AsyncLocalStorage`; path-based redaction including error payloads; a bounded, documented sampling policy that never samples errors; child loggers with inherited bindings; and a pluggable destination so tests can assert on output.

```ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export type Level = 'trace' | 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error' | 'fatal';
const SEVERITY: Record<Level, number> = { trace: 10, debug: 20, info: 30, warn: 40, error: 50, fatal: 60 };

export interface LogRecord {
  time: string;
  level: Level;
  msg: string;
  bindings: Record<string, unknown>;
  fields: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export class Logger {
  constructor(
    private state: {
      level: Level;
      bindings: Record<string, unknown>;
      sampleRate: number;              // fraction of NON-error lines kept
      sink: (r: LogRecord) => void;
      redact: string[];                // dotted paths
      base: Record<string, unknown>;
    },
    private readonly ctx = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ requestId?: string; traceId?: string }>(),
    private readonly rnd: () => number = Math.random,
  ) {}

  level(): Level { return this.state.level; }
  setLevel(l: Level) { this.state.level = l; }        // the "debug one pod" mechanism

  child(bindings: Record<string, unknown>): Logger {
    // Bindings are inherited and merged; nested objects are SHALLOW merged so a
    // child cannot clobber a parent's context.
    return new Logger(
      { ...this.state, bindings: { ...this.state.bindings, ...bindings } },
      this.ctx, this.rnd,
    );
  }

  // Run a block with request context; every log inside inherits it.
  withContext<T>(ctx: { requestId?: string; traceId?: string }, fn: () => T): T {
    return this.ctx.run({ ...this.ctx.getStore(), ...ctx }, fn);
  }

  // Attach context to an already-running async scope (an Express middleware).
  enter(ctx: { requestId?: string; traceId?: string }) {
    const merged = { ...this.ctx.getStore(), ...ctx };
    this.ctx.enterWith(merged);
    return merged;
  }

  log(level: Level, fields: Record<string, unknown>, msg: string) {
    if (SEVERITY[level] < SEVERITY[this.state.level]) return;

    // Sampling applies ONLY below `error`. Errors are the signal; sampling them
    // destroys the only evidence you have.
    if (SEVERITY[level] < SEVERITY.error && this.state.sampleRate < 1) {
      if (this.rnd() >= this.state.sampleRate) return;
    }

    const redacted = redactPaths(fields, this.state.redact);
    const store = this.ctx.getStore();
    const record: LogRecord = {
      time: new Date().toISOString(),
      level,
      msg,
      bindings: { ...this.state.base, ...this.state.bindings, ...(store ?? {}) },
      fields: redacted,
    };
    this.state.sink(record);
  }

  trace(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('trace', f, m); }
  debug(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('debug', f, m); }
  info(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('info', f, m); }
  warn(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('warn', f, m); }
  error(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('error', f, m); }
  fatal(f: Record<string, unknown>, m: string) { this.log('fatal', f, m); }
}

/** Redact by dotted/bracket path. `*.password` matches one level; `**.password` matches any depth. */
export function redactPaths(obj: Record<string, unknown>, paths: string[], censor = '[redacted]'): Record<string, unknown> {
  const rules = paths.map(parsePath);
  const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) {
    if (matches(rules, k)) { out[k] = censor; continue; }
    if (v && typeof v === 'object' && !Array.isArray(v)) {
      // A child object is only redacted wholesale if the path covers it; otherwise recurse.
      out[k] = redactPaths(v as Record<string, unknown>, paths, censor);
    } else {
      out[k] = v;
    }
  }
  return out;
}

function parsePath(p: string): string[] { return p.replace(/\[(\d+)\]/g, '.$1').split('.'); }
function matches(rules: string[][], key: string): boolean {
  const keyParts = key.split('.');
  return rules.some(rule => {
    // '**' consumes any number of levels; '*' exactly one.
    let i = 0, k = 0;
    while (i < rule.length) {
      if (rule[i] === '**') return true;
      if (k >= keyParts.length) return false;
      if (rule[i] !== '*' && rule[i] !== keyParts[k]) return false;
      i++; k++;
    }
    return i === rule.length && k === keyParts.length;
  });
}

/** A safe error serialiser: message, stack, code — never the whole object graph. */
export function errField(err: unknown) {
  if (err instanceof Error) {
    const e = err as Error & { code?: string; statusCode?: number };
    return { message: err.message, stack: err.stack, code: e.code, status: e.statusCode };
  }
  return { message: String(err) };
}

/** Wiring for real use. */
export function createLogger(opts: { level: Level; service: string; env: string; redact?: string[] }) {
  const records: LogRecord[] = [];
  const sink = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test'
    ? (r: LogRecord) => { records.push(r); }              // in-memory for assertions
    : (r: LogRecord) => { process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(r) + '\n'); };

  return {
    logger: new Logger({
      level: opts.level,
      bindings: {},
      sampleRate: opts.env === 'production' ? 0.05 : 1,
      redact: opts.redact ?? ['password', '*.password', 'token', '*.token', 'headers.authorization', 'headers.cookie', 'ssn'],
      base: { service: opts.service, env: opts.env },
      sink,
    }),
    records,   // test-only handle
  };
}
```

*Edge cases:* a log call with a field literally named `constructor` or `__proto__` (prototype pollution in a naive merge — use `Object.create(null)` for the record); an `Error` nested inside another error (`cause`); `sampleRate = 0`; a child logger whose binding must not override the parent's `service`; level switched mid-flight while a request is in progress; an `Array` field containing an object with a secret (the naive recursion above does not redact inside arrays — the real implementation must walk arrays with their index in the path); `Error.stack` being non-enumerable (JSON.stringify gives `{}` without the explicit serialiser).

*Follow-ups:* how you would compute the daily volume and set `sampleRate`; how you would add a `SlowLog` that fires once per request at a latency threshold; how you would ship logs to stdout without blocking the event loop (a transport worker thread, not synchronous `writeSync`).

---

### 3. Boundary validation: a typed parse layer for body/query/params/headers

**The contract:** every untrusted input is parsed exactly once at the edge into a typed value; the parsed value replaces the raw one; errors are RFC 9457 problem details with machine-readable codes and precise paths; unknown keys are rejected or stripped according to a per-schema policy; coercion is bounded; and the parsed result flows inward with no re-validation.

```ts
import { z } from 'zod';

// --- Primitives with explicit bounds and canonical forms --------------------
const Uuid = z.string().uuid();
const IsoDate = z.string().datetime({ offset: true }).transform(d => new Date(d));
const MoneyCents = z.number().int().nonnegative().max(100_000_000);
const PageSize = z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20);
const PageNum  = z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100_000).default(1);

// An enum for sort fields. An ALLOWLIST, because the value reaches `order by`.
const SortField = z.enum(['createdAt', 'totalCents']).default('createdAt');

// --- Shared shapes ---------------------------------------------------------
const OrderItem = z.object({
  sku: z.string().min(1).max(64).regex(/^[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9-]*$/),
  qty: z.number().int().min(1).max(100),
  unitPriceCents: MoneyCents,
}).strict();

const CreateOrder = z.object({
  customerId: Uuid,
  currency: z.enum(['USD', 'EUR', 'GBP']),
  items: z.array(OrderItem).min(1).max(50),
  couponCode: z.string().toUpperCase().regex(/^[A-Z0-9]{4,12}$/).optional(),
  placedAt: IsoDate.optional(),
}).strict();   // a `role` field in the body is a 422, not a silent privilege escalation

const ListOrders = z.object({
  limit: PageSize,
  page: PageNum,
  sort: SortField,
  order: z.enum(['asc', 'desc']).default('desc'),
  status: z.enum(['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled']).optional(),
  customerId: Uuid.optional(),
  from: IsoDate.optional(),
  to: IsoDate.optional(),
}).refine(q => !q.from || !q.to || q.from <= q.to, { message: '`from` must be before `to`', path: ['from'] });

// --- Generic parse helper --------------------------------------------------
export type ParseTarget = 'body' | 'query' | 'params' | 'headers';

export function parseInput<S extends z.ZodTypeAny>(schema: S, source: ParseTarget) {
  return (req: any, res: any, next: any) => {
    const result = schema.safeParse(req[source]);
    if (!result.success) return res.status(422).json(problem(result.error, req));
    // REPLACE, not assert. Downstream must never see the raw value.
    req[source] = result.data;
    // A parsed marker other middleware can assert on.
    req.validated ??= {};
    req.validated[source] = result.data;
    next();
  };
}

export function problem(err: z.ZodError, req: any) {
  return {
    type: 'https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error',
    title: 'Request validation failed',
    status: 422,
    traceId: req.id ?? undefined,
    // Dedupe by path: a union can produce two issues for the same field.
    errors: dedupeByPath(err.issues).map(i => ({
      path: i.path.join('.') || '(root)',
      code: i.code,
      message: i.message,
      // NEVER echo the submitted value: it leaks data and reflects payloads back.
    })),
  };
}

function dedupeByPath(issues: z.ZodIssue[]) {
  const seen = new Map<string, z.ZodIssue>();
  for (const i of issues) { const k = i.path.join('.'); if (!seen.has(k)) seen.set(k, i); }
  return [...seen.values()].sort((a, b) => a.path.join('.').localeCompare(b.path.join('.')));
}

// --- Route wiring ----------------------------------------------------------
router.post('/orders',
  parseInput(z.object({ orderId: Uuid }).strict(), 'params'),
  parseInput(CreateOrder, 'body'),
  handler);

// --- Typed handler: the parsed values are typed, so `body` is not `any` -----
type Infer<S extends z.ZodTypeAny> = z.infer<S>;
async function handler(req: { body: Infer<typeof CreateOrder> }) {
  // req.body.currency is 'USD' | 'EUR' | 'GBP', not string.
  // req.body.items[0].qty is number. No coercion happens downstream.
  return { ok: true };
}

// --- Prototype-pollution and depth guards ----------------------------------
export function assertSafeShape(value: unknown, path = '$', depth = 0) {
  if (depth > 20) throw Object.assign(new Error('too deeply nested'), { status: 422, path });
  if (!value || typeof value !== 'object') return;
  if (Array.isArray(value)) {
    if (value.length > 1000) throw Object.assign(new Error('array too long'), { status: 422, path });
    value.forEach((v, i) => assertSafeShape(v, `${path}[${i}]`, depth + 1));
    return;
  }
  for (const k of Object.keys(value as object)) {
    if (k === '__proto__' || k === 'constructor' || k === 'prototype') {
      throw Object.assign(new Error('forbidden key'), { status: 422, path: `${path}.${k}` });
    }
    assertSafeShape((value as any)[k], `${path}.${k}`, depth + 1);
  }
}
```

*Edge cases:* `?limit=1e999` → `Infinity` → fails `int()`; `?limit=abc` → `NaN` → fails; `?limit=` → `0` → fails `min(1)` (good, but if you want "empty means default" you must preprocess); a body with 200 items → `max(50)`; a body that is an array instead of an object → `invalid_type`; duplicate JSON keys → last wins in most parsers (so a signature check on the raw bytes is the only defence); `null` sent for an optional string → `invalid_type` unless `.nullable()`; a very long `couponCode` → regex runs on the whole string, so bound length *before* the pattern; a unicode slug that NFKC-normalises to a different string.

*Follow-ups:* how you would generate the OpenAPI request schema from these Zod schemas (`zod-to-openapi`); how you would validate an entire route in one pass and produce one merged error; how you would version a request schema so an old client keeps working while a new one gets new fields.

### 4. Keyset pagination: signed opaque cursors, stable under concurrent writes

**The contract:** the response envelope never varies; the cursor is opaque, signed, versioned, filter-bound, and tamper-evident; the predicate is a row-wise tuple comparison on a unique tiebreaker; the index matches the sort; `hasNextPage` costs no `COUNT`; invalid or foreign cursors produce a clean `400`; and the pager returns each row exactly once while rows are being inserted and deleted.

```ts
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

export type Cursor = { v: 1; ts: string; id: string; dir: 'asc' | 'desc'; fh: string };

export class PagerError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly code: 'malformed_cursor' | 'invalid_cursor' | 'cursor_version' | 'cursor_filter') {
    super(code);
  }
}

export function encodeCursor(c: Cursor, secret: string): string {
  const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(c)).toString('base64url');
  const sig = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest('base64url');
  return `${body}.${sig}`;
}

export function decodeCursor(raw: string, secret: string): Cursor {
  const dot = raw.lastIndexOf('.');
  if (dot < 1) throw new PagerError('malformed_cursor');
  const body = raw.slice(0, dot), sig = raw.slice(dot + 1);
  const expected = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest();
  const given = Buffer.from(sig, 'base64url');
  if (given.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(given, expected)) throw new PagerError('invalid_cursor');
  let c: Cursor;
  try { c = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(body, 'base64url').toString()); }
  catch { throw new PagerError('malformed_cursor'); }
  if (c.v !== 1) throw new PagerError('cursor_version');
  if (typeof c.ts !== 'string' || typeof c.id !== 'string') throw new PagerError('malformed_cursor');
  return c;
}

// A stable fingerprint of the filter set. A cursor from one query replayed
// against another silently returns the wrong window, so bind them together.
export function filterHash(filters: Record<string, unknown>): string {
  const canonical = JSON.stringify(filters, Object.keys(filters).sort());
  return createHmac('sha256', canonical).update('filter').digest('base64url').slice(0, 12);
}

export type Page<T> = {
  data: T[];
  pageInfo: { hasNextPage: boolean; endCursor: string | null };
};

export interface PageOptions {
  tenantId: string;
  limit: number;                       // already bounded by validation, 1..100
  cursor?: string;
  dir: 'asc' | 'desc';
  sort: 'createdAt' | 'totalCents';    // allowlisted upstream
  filters: Record<string, unknown>;
  secret: string;
}

export async function paginate<T extends { id: string; createdAt: Date; totalCents: number }>(
  db: Db, opts: PageOptions,
): Promise<Page<T>> {
  const fh = filterHash({ ...opts.filters, sort: opts.sort });
  let anchor: Cursor | undefined;

  if (opts.cursor) {
    anchor = decodeCursor(opts.cursor, opts.secret);
    if (anchor.dir !== opts.dir) throw new PagerError('cursor_filter');
    if (anchor.fh !== fh) throw new PagerError('cursor_filter');   // replay across queries is refused
  }

  const col = opts.sort === 'totalCents' ? 'total_cents' : 'created_at';
  const dir = opts.dir === 'asc' ? 'ASC' : 'DESC';
  const cmp = opts.dir === 'asc' ? '>' : '<';

  // Row-wise tuple comparison: (a, b) < (c, d)  ==  a < c OR (a = c AND b < d).
  // The `id` tiebreaker is what makes it total. Without it, rows sharing the
  // sort value are silently skipped.
  const where = opts.filters.status
    ? `${col} is not null and status = $status` : 'true';
  const params: unknown[] = [opts.tenantId, opts.limit + 1];
  const anchorClause = anchor ? ` and (${col}, id) ${cmp} ($anchorCol, $anchorId)` : '';
  if (anchor) { params.push(anchor.ts, anchor.id); }

  const sqlText = `
    select * from orders
    where tenant_id = $1 and deleted_at is null and ${where}${anchorClause}
    order by ${col} ${dir}, id ${dir}
    limit $2
  `;
  const bind = (v: unknown) => `$${params.push(v)}`;

  const rows = await db.query(
    sqlText
      .replace('$1', bind(opts.tenantId))
      .replace('$2', bind(opts.limit + 1))
      .replace('$status', bind(opts.filters.status))
      .replace('$anchorCol', bind(anchor!.ts))
      .replace('$anchorId', bind(anchor!.id)),
    params,
  ) as T[];

  const hasNextPage = rows.length > opts.limit;
  const data = hasNextPage ? rows.slice(0, opts.limit) : rows;
  const last = data.at(-1);
  const endCursor = last
    ? encodeCursor({ v: 1, ts: last.createdAt.toISOString(), id: last.id, dir: opts.dir, fh }, opts.secret)
    : null;

  return { data, pageInfo: { hasNextPage, endCursor } };
}

// --- Index that serves it. Without `id` in the key, Postgres sorts every page.
export const ORDERS_INDEX = `
  create index concurrently orders_tenant_created_id
    on orders (tenant_id, created_at desc, id desc) where deleted_at is null;
`;

/** Offset paginator, for the cases that genuinely need it — with a hard cap. */
export const MAX_OFFSET = 10_000;
export function assertOffsetAllowed(offset: number) {
  // Deep offsets degrade to a full scan. Refuse rather than let a client
  // burn 30s of database CPU.
  if (offset > MAX_OFFSET) {
    throw Object.assign(new Error('offset too deep; use a cursor'), { status: 400, code: 'offset_too_deep' });
  }
}
```

*Edge cases:* two rows with identical `created_at` (the tiebreaker test — without `id` you lose one); the anchor row is deleted between pages (values still work, which is the point); a cursor from tenant A replayed against tenant B (the `fh` hash includes tenant-scoped filters, and the query always includes `tenant_id = $1`); a tampered cursor (HMAC mismatch → `invalid_cursor`, not a 500); a cursor from a different sort or direction (`cursor_filter`); an empty result set on page 1 (`endCursor: null`); `limit + 1` on the *last* page returning exactly `limit`; a cursor older than the retention window (rows may have been purged, so the client gets a shorter page — acceptable, and it is why you version cursors).

*Follow-ups:* how you would add a "jump to page 40" affordance without offset (a count cache plus a `seek to id` lookup); how you would make a snapshot for an export (`repeatable read`, or materialise ids first); how you would paginate a `LEFT JOIN` without the duplicate-row problem.

### 5. Soft delete with restore, purge, and a retention job

**The contract:** live rows are hidden by a predicate that cannot be forgotten; unique constraints apply only to live rows; restore enforces the unique constraint and revokes credentials; purge is batched, resumable, rate-limited, and respects `legal_hold`; and every state change is audited.

```sql
-- Schema. The partial unique index is the whole ballgame.
alter table customers
  add column deleted_at  timestamptz null,
  add column deleted_by  uuid null references users(id),
  add column legal_hold  boolean not null default false,
  add column purge_after timestamptz null;

drop index customers_email_key;                        -- the trap
create unique index customers_email_live_key on customers (email) where deleted_at is null;

create index customers_tenant_live
  on customers (tenant_id, created_at desc, id desc) where deleted_at is null;
```
```ts
export class SoftDeleteService {
  constructor(private db: Db, private audit: AuditService, private crypto: Crypto) {}

  // The scope lives HERE, in one place. Nothing else in the codebase writes SQL.
  async listLive(tenantId: string, q: { status?: string; limit: number; cursor?: string }) {
    return this.db.query(`
      select id, email, display_name, created_at from customers
      where tenant_id = $1 and deleted_at is null and ($2::text is null or status = $2)
      order by created_at desc, id desc
      limit $3
    `, [tenantId, q.status ?? null, q.limit]);
  }

  async softDelete(tenantId: string, id: string, actorId: string, reason: string) {
    return this.db.transaction(async tx => {
      const { rows } = await tx.query(`
        update customers set deleted_at = now(), deleted_by = $3, purge_after = now() + interval '30 days'
        where id = $1 and tenant_id = $2 and deleted_at is null
        returning *
      `, [id, tenantId, actorId]);
      if (!rows.length) throw new NotFound('customer');
      // Revoke credentials NOW, not on purge. A deleted user must not keep a
      // live session for 30 days.
      await tx.query(`update sessions set revoked_at = now() where customer_id = $1 and revoked_at is null`, [id]);
      await tx.query(`update api_keys  set revoked_at = now() where customer_id = $1 and revoked_at is null`, [id]);
      await this.audit.append(tx, { actorId, tenantId, action: 'customer.deleted', entity: 'customer', id, reason, after: rows[0] });
      return rows[0];
    });
  }

  async restore(tenantId: string, id: string, actorId: string, reason: string) {
    return this.db.transaction(async tx => {
      // The partial unique index may reject this: someone may have re-registered
      // the same email while this row was deleted. That is a REAL conflict and
      // must surface, not be swallowed.
      const live = await tx.query(`select id from customers where email = (select email from customers where id = $1) and deleted_at is null`, [id]);
      if (live.length) {
        throw new Conflict('email_taken', `Cannot restore: email now belongs to customer ${live[0].id}`);
      }
      const { rows } = await tx.query(`
        update customers set deleted_at = null, deleted_by = null, purge_after = null
        where id = $1 and tenant_id = $2 and deleted_at is not null returning *
      `, [id, tenantId]);
      if (!rows.length) throw new NotFound('customer');
      // A restore must NOT resurrect access. Old sessions stay revoked.
      await this.audit.append(tx, { actorId, tenantId, action: 'customer.restored', entity: 'customer', id, reason, after: rows[0] });
      return rows[0];
    });
  }

  /** Anonymise instead of delete: erases PII while keeping the financial record. */
  async anonymise(tenantId: string, customerId: string, actorId: string) {
    return this.db.transaction(async tx => {
      await tx.query(`
        update customers set
          email = 'erased+' || id::text || '@invalid.example',
          display_name = 'Erased',
          phone = null, address = null, avatar_url = null,
          deleted_at = now(), deleted_by = $3,
          anonymised_at = now()
        where id = $1 and tenant_id = $2
      `, [customerId, tenantId, actorId]);
      // Records with a legal or accounting basis are retained WITHOUT personal fields.
      await tx.query(`update invoices set billing_name = 'Erased', billing_address = null where customer_id = $1`, [customerId]);
      await this.audit.append(tx, { actorId, tenantId, action: 'customer.anonymised', entity: 'customer', id: customerId });
    });
  }
}

/** The retention job: batched, resumable, rate-limited, hold-aware. */
export async function purgeExpired(batchSize = 1_000, maxBatches = 50, pauseMs = 50) {
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < maxBatches; i++) {
    // Keyset loop: never OFFSET, so it resumes correctly and holds no long locks.
    // legal_hold is checked per row, so a hold on one row does not block the batch.
    const { rows } = await db.query(`
      with doomed as (
        select id from customers
        where deleted_at is not null
          and purge_after is not null and purge_after < now()
          and legal_hold = false
        order by purge_after
        limit $1
        for update skip locked        -- concurrent purge workers do not collide
      )
      delete from customers c using doomed where c.id = doomed.id
      returning c.id
    `, [batchSize]);

    if (!rows.length) break;
    total += rows.length;
    await sleep(pauseMs);            // yield; do not monopolise the table
  }
  return { purged: total };
}
```

*Edge cases:* re-registering a soft-deleted email (partial index makes it work); restoring into that same email (the `Conflict` above); purging while a transaction holds a lock (`skip locked` skips, does not block); a `legal_hold` row inside a batch (skipped, not deleted); a restore older than the retention window (the row is gone → `NotFound`, and the error message must not confirm it ever existed); concurrent soft-delete of the same row (the `and deleted_at is null` guard means the second call gets zero rows → `NotFound`, which is correct); a purge of a parent with children (FK restrict → the batch fails; decide per relationship whether children are cascaded or anonymised first).

*Follow-ups:* how you would make the purge job runnable in parallel safely (it already is, via `skip locked`); how you would report on "users scheduled for purge this week" for a support team; how you would implement legal hold as a UI action with an expiry.
